avalanche.e: From French avalanche, from Franco-Provençal (Savoy) avalançhe, blend of aval (“downhill”) and standard lavençhe, from Vulgar Latin *labanka (compare Occitan lavanca, Italian valanga), of uncertain origin, perhaps an alteration of Late Latin lābīna (“landslide”) (compare Franco-Provençal (Dauphiné) lavino, Romansh lavina), from Latin lābēs, from lābor (“to slip, slide”).

s.d: a slide of large masses of snow and ice and mud down a mountain
a sudden appearance of an overwhelming number of things

s.d: A large mass or body of snow and ice sliding swiftly down a mountain side, or falling down a precipice.
x: They were drinking from a fountain / That was pouring like an avalanche / Coming down the mountain

s.d: A fall of earth, rocks, etc., similar to that of an avalanche of snow or ice.
A sudden, great, or irresistible descent or influx; anything like an avalanche in suddenness and overwhelming quantity.

s.d: To come down upon; to overwhelm.

x: Then another misfortune avalanched itself upon me, before even I had fully taken in the extent of the first.
